report.summary: The Financial Times argues AI has moved from laboratory to battlefield, making autonomous targeting and AI-assisted command a defining feature of modern warfare.
report.background: The FT's full article sits behind a paywall, but the headline points to a shift analysts have tracked for years. Military AI moved from experiment to operations in stages: Google's Project Maven (2017), drone-dominated fighting in Nagorno-Karabakh (2020), Ukraine's use of AI-assisted targeting and video analysis from 2022, and reported AI targeting systems used in Gaza in 2023–24. The Pentagon's Replicator initiative, the Chief Digital and AI Office, and China's push toward "intelligentised warfare" have since institutionalised these tools. Venture capital has poured into a new defence-tech sector, with Anduril, Helsing, Shield AI and Palantir becoming significant suppliers. Governance has lagged badly: UN talks on lethal autonomous weapons remain stalled, and the 2023 US political declaration on responsible military AI is non-binding. The FT's framing suggests the inflection point has passed — AI is now doctrine, not prototype.
key_points: AI has crossed from pilot projects into standing military doctrine. Sensor-fusion and targeting software, much of it commercial, now compresses the sensor-to-shooter loop from hours to minutes, embedding algorithms directly into kill chains rather than merely advising human analysts.

Cheap drones plus AI edge computing have democratised precision strike. FPV drones with terminal guidance and jamming-resistant links let small units hit targets once reserved for expensive air power, and Ukraine's million-drone-per-year output shows how industrial scale changes the economics of war.

Command, control and intelligence are being automated too. Large language models and machine-learning tools are used for battle planning, wargaming, translation and intelligence triage — raising concerns about automation bias, opaque recommendations and accountability when humans rubber-stamp machine output.

Governance is not keeping pace. UN talks on lethal autonomous weapons remain deadlocked, no binding treaty exists, and export controls on advanced chips are porous, meaning both state and non-state actors can acquire capable AI systems.

A new defence-tech capital cycle has formed. Billions in venture funding have created challenger primes alongside Lockheed and RTX, while big-tech cloud contracts and employee ethics protests have made military work a central strategic question for the AI industry.
report.impact: For the AI industry, defence is becoming one of the largest, least cyclical buyers, reshaping procurement, valuations and hiring, and pushing edge inference, robust perception and reinforcement learning to the frontier. For developers, dual-use work brings export-control obligations, security clearances and ethical exposure, while open-weight models raise real proliferation risks. For ordinary users, the same technologies leak into policing, border control and surveillance, and AI-generated disinformation, drone incidents and escalation risk make warfare's costs visible far from any front line.
report.tools: To follow up: Palantir Foundry/AIP, Anduril's Lattice and Menace, Helsing, Shield AI Hivemind and the Pentagon's Maven Smart System/GIDE for military software. Open-source entry points include ROS 2, PX4 and ArduPilot for autonomy, and Ultralytics YOLO for edge vision. For governance tracking, watch SIPRI, the IISS Military Balance, the UN CCW talks and the Stop Killer Robots coalition.
